topic: Pakistan Declares Open War on Afghanistan's Taliban Government

subtopics.title: Regime changes in Afghanistan (1973-2021)
subtopics.summary: Afghanistan's political history since 1973 has seen a series of regimes, each shaped by outside powers. The monarchy ended in 1973 and was followed by Soviet-backed communist rule, and Soviet military intervention in 1979 drew Pakistan into supporting Afghan Mujahideen factions. Civil war after 1992 led to Taliban rule, which ended with the US intervention of 2001, and the Taliban regained full control after the US withdrawal in August 2021.
facts: Afghanistan's monarchy ended in 1973.
The nationalist regime was followed by communist rule backed by the Soviet Union.
In 1979 the Soviet Union intervened militarily in Afghanistan.
Pakistan supported Afghan Mujahideen factions during the Soviet intervention.
President Najibullah's government collapsed in 1992, triggering civil war.
The Taliban emerged in 1994 and captured Kabul in 1996.
Pakistan was one of the few countries to recognise the Taliban regime.
After the 9/11 attacks, the United States invaded Afghanistan and overthrew the Taliban.
The new Islamic Republic struggled with insurgency and corruption.
After the US withdrawal in August 2021, the Taliban regained full control.

subtopics.title: Factors behind the open war
subtopics.summary: Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab-Lil-Haq on Afghan military bases, and Afghanistan retaliated with airstrikes on Pakistani targets. The escalation grew out of long-standing disputes over cross-border militancy, the Durand Line and border fencing. Clashes at disputed checkpoints turned these tensions into direct military confrontation.
facts: Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab-Lil-Haq on Afghan military bases.
Afghanistan retaliated with airstrikes on Nur Khan Airbase (Rawalpindi) and 12th Division HQ (Quetta).
The Afghan Taliban is allegedly sheltering Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
TTP is accused of launching cross-border attacks inside Pakistan.
Pakistan recognises the Durand Line as a permanent international border.
Afghan governments have historically disputed the legitimacy of the Durand Line.
Pakistan's border fencing has been resisted by Afghan forces.
Repeated Torkham crossing closures hurt Afghan trade and deepened mistrust.
Pakistan's 'strategic depth' doctrine has been eroded by the Taliban's outreach to India.

subtopics.title: India-Afghanistan ties and projects
subtopics.summary: India and Afghanistan share historic links, including Gandhara's place among the Mahajanapadas of the Vedic Age and the Bamiyan Buddhas. Afghanistan is also a crossroad between South Asia and Central Asia, and India has supported its energy, agriculture, drinking water and democratic institutions through projects. The Zaranj-Delaram Highway helps Afghanistan reach Iran's Chabahar Port while bypassing Pakistan.
facts: Gandhara, part of modern-day Afghanistan, was one of 16 Mahajanapadas in the Vedic Age.
The Bamiyan Buddhas highlight the influence of Buddhism in Afghanistan.
Afghanistan is a crossroad between South Asia and Central Asia, and between South Asia and the Middle East.
TAPI (Peace) Pipeline: a 1814 km gas pipeline from the Galkynysh Gas Field in Turkmenistan through Afghanistan, Pakistan and India.
Salma Dam (Afghan-India Friendship Dam), 2016, in Herat Province, supports energy and agriculture.
Zaranj-Delaram Highway (2009) connects Afghanistan to Iran's Chabahar Port and was built by India's Border Roads Organization.
Shahtoot Dam Project (2021) aims to provide drinking water to Kabul.
Afghan Parliament Building (2015), built by India, symbolises India's commitment to Afghan democracy.

subtopics.title: Implications for India
subtopics.summary: The Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict has several implications for India, touching its western border, its security and its trade routes. Escalation may reduce Pakistan's infiltration pressure along the LoC, but prolonged instability could let ISIS-K regroup and jeopardise India's access to the INSTC. India condemned Pakistan's attacks and reaffirmed support for Afghanistan's sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence.
facts: India condemned Pakistan's attacks and reaffirmed support for Afghanistan's sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence.
LoC relief: escalation on the western border may compel Pakistan to reduce infiltration pressure along the LoC.
Terror spillover: prolonged instability risks allowing ISIS-K to regroup and expand across South Asia.
Connectivity risks: the conflict jeopardises India's access to the INSTC and Central Asian trade outreach.
Refugee pressure: a full-scale conflict risks an Afghan refugee inflow onto India's borders.

quizzes.passage: Pakistan and Afghanistan have shared a difficult relationship for decades, shaped by changes of government inside Afghanistan and by the border between the two countries. Afghanistan's monarchy ended in 1973 and was followed by communist rule backed by the Soviet Union. Pakistan supported Afghan Mujahideen factions during the period of Soviet military intervention, and later became one of the few countries to recognise the Taliban regime. After the Taliban regained full control in 2021, Pakistan initially welcomed the development, expecting strategic alignment. Tensions soon resurfaced, however, as cross-border militancy continued. Pakistan alleges that the Afghan Taliban is sheltering the TTP, while Afghan governments have historically disputed the legitimacy of the Durand Line, which Pakistan treats as a permanent international border. Afghanistan argues that the agreement behind the line was signed under colonial pressure, while Pakistan says it inherited the boundary after independence in 1947. Clashes at disputed checkpoints escalated into direct military confrontation, and the fighting drew a sharp response from India, which condemned Pakistan's attacks. Pakistan's traditional doctrine of strategic depth has also been eroded, since the Taliban has reached out to India and reduced Pakistan's leverage over Kabul. The result is a conflict in which border disputes, militancy and trade disruption reinforce one another.

quizzes.passage: India's relationship with Afghanistan rests on historical, cultural and developmental foundations. Gandhara, a region that is part of modern-day Afghanistan, was one of the Mahajanapadas of the Vedic Age, and the Bamiyan Buddhas reflect the influence of Buddhism in the country. Afghanistan is also strategically important, because it acts as a crossroad between South Asia and Central Asia as well as between South Asia and the Middle East. Over the years, India has backed projects that support Afghanistan's energy, agriculture and drinking water needs, as well as its democratic institutions. Dams, roads and public buildings are among the projects India has built or helped build. One gas pipeline would carry natural gas from Turkmenistan through Afghanistan and Pakistan to India, while another highway gives Afghanistan a route to a port in Iran that bypasses Pakistan. India has also engaged the Taliban regime at a senior diplomatic level, and these ties have continued even as Afghanistan's political leadership has changed. Afghanistan's position on the border differs, since it does not officially recognise the Durand Line. Repeated closures of the Torkham crossing have also hurt Afghan trade and pushed Kabul toward Iranian routes, which shows how trade and border policy are linked. Taken together, India's engagement covers history, development and trade.
